title: ‘Evil Dead’ Star Bruce Campbell Says He Has 5 Years to Live After Incurable Cancer Diagnosis: I’m ‘Dying’ but ‘I’m Moving On’
description:
“Evil Dead” star Bruce Campbell is opening up about his battle with cancer, revealing that he’s been given about five years to live.

	Back in March
body:
“Evil Dead” star Bruce Campbell is opening up about his battle with cancer, revealing that he’s been given about five years to live.

	Back in March, Campbell revealed he had been diagnosed with a cancer that was “treatable but not curable.”

	“These days, when someone is having a health issue, it’s referred to as an ‘opportunity,’ so let’s go with that — I’m having one of those,” he wrote on X in March. “It’s also called a type of cancer that’s ‘treatable’ not ‘curable.’ I apologize if that’s a shock – it was to me too.”
	

	Campbell didn’t go into detail about what type of cancer he’d been diagnosed with, but wrote that “professionally, a few things will have to change. Appearances and cons and work in general need to take back seat to treatment. My plan is to get as well as I possibly can over the summer so that I can tour with my new movie ‘Ernie & Emma’ this fall.”


	On Wednesday’s episode of “The Adam Carolla Show,” Campbell opened up more about his diagnosis and treatment while also discussing his new movie.

	“I’m in a five-year prognosis,” he said. “With the type of cancer that I have, which I don’t want to get into, the current thing is a five-year deal.” When Carolla asked if that meant Campbell had five years to live, the actor replied “give or take.”

	“It’s a fascinating thing that takes place because [cancer] messes with your head, too. I’ve decided though, pretty specifically, to live with it, not die from it,” he added. “You can go down a massive rabbit hole. The cancer rabbit hole is enormous. You can go into focus groups of 10,000 guys who have exactly what you have. I won’t touch it with a 10-foot pole.”
	

	Campbell serves as director, writer, producer and lead actor in “Ernie & Emma,” in which he plays a widower scattering his late wife’s ashes, reflecting on their relationship together and confronting his grief.

	“It’s a very fascinating time of having a movie about a guy who’s spreading his wife’s ashes, who died, made by a guy who’s dying,” he told Carolla.

	Campbell, who starred as the chainsaw-wielding Ash Williams in director Sam Raimi’s original “Evil Dead” trilogy, executive produced this summer’s installment in the horror franchise, “Evil Dead Burn.” He’s also an EP on the next movie, 2028’s “Evil Dead Wrath.”

	“I’m moving on. I got a movie to promote. And when I promote this movie, I have nothing. I’m free and clear when I promote this movie mentally,” Campbell said. “You have to make this decision of, ‘Well, OK, but do I have to stop everything that I’m doing because of this?’ Well, no.”

	Watch his full interview below.

schema.headline: ‘Evil Dead’ Star Bruce Campbell Says He Has 5 Years to Live After Incurable Cancer Diagnosis: I’m ‘Dying’ but ‘I’m Moving On’

title: Robert Pattinson Kisses Suki Waterhouse as ‘Primetime’ Rocks Venice With 7-Minute Standing Ovation
description: “Primetime,” a thriller starring Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, made its debut at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday
body:
“Primetime,” a thriller starring Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, made its debut at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday to an enthusiastic seven-minute ovation.

	Venice went fully in for Pattinson’s immersive performance as Hansen, the “Dateline” journalist and host who sets out to make television history with “To Catch a Predator.” And one of the biggest fans in attendance? Pattinson’s partner Suki Waterhouse, who cheered perhaps loudest during the seven-minute standing ovation and leaned forward and kissed Pattinson on the lips as the crowd applauded his tour-de-force performance. (In Venice, actors are seated in the front row of the balcony and their partners must sit a row behind them.) As the ovation stretched into its sixth minute, the audience began chanting for director Lance Oppenheim and singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers, who makes her acting debut in the film. Skyler Gisondo and Merritt Wever also star.
	

	Based on Luke Dittrich’s 2007 Esquire article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” “Primetime” follows the production of the popular series, in which Hansen attempted to confront child sexual predators in complex sting operations.


	Massive crowds outside the Palazzo del Cinema were chanting “Robert! Robert! Robert!” as they baked in the sun on a brutally hot Saturday afternoon. Pattinson, Gisando and Bridgers dutifully signed autographs and posed for tons of selfies with fans while Waterhouse made small talk with producers off to the side of the action. Pattinson dabbed the sweat off his forehead with napkins before posing for a cast photo. Former NBC chief Jeff Zucker, who appears in the movie as himself, also walked the red carpet, as did producer Ari Aster.
	

	“Primetime” marks Oppenheim’s feature debut, having previously helmed acclaimed documentaries such as “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire.” A24 will release “Primetime” in theaters on Sept. 25.

	Hansen has been vocal in his criticisms about “Primetime,” saying he wasn’t involved in the creative process and hadn’t seen the movie. He called Pattinson’s portrayal “overly dramatic” and questioned the studio’s “motive” in dramatizing the making of the hit reality series. Hansen has also stressed that “Primetime” isn’t a literal account of his career and that he wasn’t consulted during the making of the movie. 

	“He’s saying things I never said and doing things I never did, and that’s not who I am. I’m a nice guy, except when it comes to criminals and predators,” Hansen previously said. “I think people should remember that it is a work of fiction, only based on real-life events.”

	At a press conference earlier on Saturday, Pattinson suggested that Hansen could come around once he sees the film. “Obviously, I hope he likes the movie,” Pattinson said. “There’s something electrifying about him. I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment.”

	“Primetime” continues a banner year for Pattinson, who stars in such high-profile films as this spring’s indie hit “The Drama,” Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” and Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming tentpole “Dune: Part III.” And Pattinson’s schedule remains packed: He jetted to Lido from London, where he is currently filming “The Batman: Part II,” reprising his role as reclusive billionaire-turned-vigilante Bruce Wayne.

	“When you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” Pattinson said at the presser. Plus, he joked, “I just had a baby. I had no desire to go out at night. So suddenly I had twice as much time, which was helpful.”

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson Kisses Suki Waterhouse as ‘Primetime’ Rocks Venice With 7-Minute Standing Ovation

title: ‘It Will Happen Tonight’ Review: Louis Garrel and Jasmine Trinca Follow Each Other Through the Years In a Light and Predictable Romcom
description: Not everything labeled “old-fashioned” needs to carry negative connotations. A handwritten letter, your grandma’s rice pudding, the cocktail — all n
body:
Not everything labeled “old-fashioned” needs to carry negative connotations. A handwritten letter, your grandma’s rice pudding, the cocktail — all nice old-fashioned things. But the moment Alberto Iglesias’ sweet music flows out of the speakers at the start of “It Will Happen Tonight,” “old-fashioned” starts veering perilously into dowdy territory. When the camera zooms out as a couple kiss by the sea, things are heading swiftly towards fusty, and that inexorable journey continues through a Bruce Springsteen concert, a cutesy fantasy group dance to The Rolling Stones’ “She’s a Rainbow,” and pretty much everything else in Nanni Moretti’s latest Venice competition entry.
	

	Though based on the short story collection “Hungry Heart” by Israeli novelist Eshkol Nevo, this is pure Moretti, turning on those moments in people’s lives when there’s a clear fork in the road and a path is chosen, whether right or wrong. Here eminently likeable Matteo (Louis Garrel) and Greta (Jasmine Trinca) casually meet when already attached to partners, think about each other for years, and wonder whether they’ve made the right life choices. 


	Unlike Celine Song’s “Past Lives,” an adult film about “what might have been” whose emotional core lies in its intelligence and its refusal to sentimentalize, “It Will Happen Tonight” leans in heavily towards the kind of lightweight romance that, for better or worse, feels out of place in today’s film festival world. While for the home crowd this is likely to be one of Moretti’s most popular movies in a long time, it’s hard to gauge how it will be received elsewhere. After all, aren’t paper-thin intrusive mothers and old Viagra-joking fathers just a wee bit passé?
	

	Matteo’s Norwegian girlfriend Thea (Melina Åkerman) is pregnant and not keen on moving from Oslo to Rome, especially when his visiting mamma Agnese (Angela Finocchiaro) tells her she’s not fit to be a mother. Once Gregorio is born and the couple fly to Rome, Thea looks from the airport exit doors at Matteo’s family ignoring her and wisely decides to turn around, leaving the baby. Meanwhile in Mumbai, Greta’s boyfriend Carlo (Edoardo Purgatori) proposes in a very public way, but she can’t go through with it and instead calls daddy (Moretti himself) to get her out of there.

	Seven years later — yes, this is the kind of movie that jumps seven, and seven, and then three — Matteo’s playing tennis with his brother Antonio (Andrea Lattanzi) when in walks Greta, looking stunning in a white dress. She kicks off her heels and takes up a racket as the music swells, the slow-mo closeups begin, and for Matteo it’s love at first sight. The problem is, she’s getting married next door to Federico (Antonio De Matteo), with whom she has a daughter, Anna (Elena-Marie Cicone).

	This lovely vision in white won’t leave his mind, though he has no way of knowing who she is and besides, he’s got a dying father, Olivier (Hippolyte Girardot), to worry about. But the grim reaper can’t get him until father and son go to a Springsteen concert in San Sebastián, where randy Olivier has sex with the hotel receptionist (played for very poor laughs) and then, for reasons best known to Moretti, the stadium scenes linger through most of “Hungry Heart” and “Because the Night,” treating us to Garrel and Girardot swaying to the music and not much else. On the plane back to Rome, Olivier unsurprisingly gives up the ghost, preceded two seconds earlier by non-diegetic piano music superfluously clueing us in to what’s just about to happen.

	San Sebastián is also where Matteo gets another glimpse of Greta, in town because she’s got a part in a movie there. This is the most problematic scene in the film: She’s wearing convincing aging prosthetics for her role (which is why Matteo doesn’t recognize her at first), frantically searching for her daughter Anna, who’s wandered off. When the child is found, she’s whispering to a little girl covered in flies who appears to be Roma. Surely Moretti should have realized the offensiveness of showing a street child crawling with insects, her mother oblivious, as if this is normal for “such people.” While designed to convey the idea of Anna as a child with a troubled inner life, the sequence goes nowhere and is never explained, nor does it fit with her later depiction as a depressed adolescent.
	

	Seven years later, Matteo and Greta have a meet-cute in a café and he reveals his ongoing obsession. She’s got three kids, he’s married to Olivier’s former doctor Cristina (Elena Lietti), but despite her initial rejection of a tryst, the two embark on a passionate affair in his father’s old apartment, conveniently left empty all these years. Will they have the courage to leave their former lives and embrace the love they should have grabbed earlier? You’ll need to wait three more years to find out, but if you don’t already know where this is heading, you’ve not seen many movies.

schema.headline: ‘It Will Happen Tonight’ Review: Louis Garrel and Jasmine Trinca Follow Each Other Through the Years In a Light and Predictable Romcom

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Is Fastest Film to Cross $900 Million at Domestic Box Office
description: Two action flicks, Paramount’s “By Any Means” and A24’s “Onslaught,” arrived in theaters on Friday. But neither could dethrone “Spider-Man: Brand Ne
body:
Two action flicks, Paramount’s “By Any Means” and A24’s “Onslaught,” arrived in theaters on Friday. But neither could dethrone “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which remains No. 1 in its sixth weekend in theaters.

	“Spider-Man” added $3.9 million on Friday, pushing it past the mind-boggling milestone of $900 million domestically. It’s now the fastest movie to cross the benchmark — doing so in just 36 days — and it beats the 50-day record set by 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” The Marvel-Sony tentpole is projected to make $22 million over the four-day Labor Day weekend, pushing its domestic total to $922 million. It’s only a matter of time until “Brand New Day” crosses $936 million and passes “The Force Awakens” as the highest-grossing domestic film of all time.
	

	“By Any Means” performed the best of the two newcomers, earning $2.7 million domestically on Friday to finish fourth behind “Spider-Man,” “The Odyssey” and “Coyote vs. Acme.” Through the long weekend, the ’60s thriller is expected to make $8.5 million. Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Mark Wahlberg headline the film, which sees a young FBI agent recruit a mafia hitman to help investigate the murders of civil rights leaders in 1960s Mississippi. Nicole Beharie, Josh Lucas, LisaGay Hamilton and LaChanze also star. Elegance Bratton directs with a screenplay by Sascha Penn.


	“Onslaught” is failing to connect after only grossing $770,000 on Friday; it’s on pace to pull in just $2.3 million by Monday. Adria Arjona leads the action movie as Celeste, an army sniper who must protect her daughter from a squad of genetically engineered super soldiers. Other cast members include Dan Stevens, Eric Wareheim, Reginald VelJohnson, Michael Biehn, Blake Kennedy and Alex Pereira. “Godzilla vs. Kong” filmmaker Adam Wingard directs the film with a script by Simon Barrett.
	

	Another July holdover, Universal’s “The Odyssey,” grossed $3 million on Friday, vaulting it to second place. Through Monday, it should pull in $16.4 million, pushing its North American haul to $588 million.

	Ketchup Entertainment’s “Coyote vs. Acme,” which also launched last week, fared much better in its second weekend. On Friday, it collected $2.6 million, and by the end of the weekend, it should pull in about $15.3 million. That figure notches up the domestic total for the Looney Tunes comedy to $37.8 million.

	20th Century’s “The Dog Stars” continues to struggle as it enters its second weekend. The dystopian drama made just $720,000 on Friday. By the end of its sophomore weekend, “The Dog Stars” is expected to earn $3.7 million, down from its disastrous $8 million opening.

schema.headline: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Is Fastest Film to Cross $900 Million at Domestic Box Office

title: Teens Seek to Heal Wounds Through Macabre Rituals in Jannis Lenz’s ‘Oasis,’ With Hints of the Influence of Jessica Hausner, Michael Haneke
description: Three teenagers, unclothed, stand close to one another in a forest, gently caressing the wounds they have inflicted on one another. This is the clim
body:
Three teenagers, unclothed, stand close to one another in a forest, gently caressing the wounds they have inflicted on one another. This is the climactic moment in “Oasis,” a film that at times feels like a Grimms Brothers fairytale, and, at others, an all-too-real vision of modern-day youth in crisis.

	If you were told that the German director, Jannis Lenz, was tutored by Jessica Hausner and was an assistant to Michael Haneke, then you’d get a sense of the influences at play in the film — his debut feature — which has its world premiere on Sunday in the Horizons section of Venice Film Festival.
	

	While Lenz acknowledges the influence Hausner and Haneke have had on him, he is keen to state he has his own approach to filmmaking. “It would be strange if [the time spent with them] wouldn’t have left an influence. But the way we work as filmmakers is very different, and the final results too. I think my way of working is much more open. I try to have more openness with the actors, with improvisation,” he tells Variety.


	He does, though, share his mentors’ love of “precision,” he says. In his case, this is mainly evident during the preparatory stage. “I prepare myself very precisely, otherwise it would be chaos later on,” he says. However, once the filming starts, you should “be willing to let yourself be surprised,” he says.

	The film begins with Andy, a newcomer to his high school in Southern Germany, being caught on camera threatening other students, and as a result he is faced with expulsion. His only friend is Lukas, the son of a teacher at the school, with whom he escapes to the forest where they engage in paintball combat.
	

	For the boys, the forest is “a place where they can retreat to,” says the director. Here, they find “some kind of a space that isn’t part of a rigid system.”

	As pressure builds on Andy from the other students, their parents and the school staff, he and Lukas find an unexpected ally in Maya, who attends a different school — one that specializes in music and the performing arts.

	While the boys had previously indulged in cliched displays of machismo, Maya helps them explore their vulnerability and sensuality, while at the same time participating in rituals of physical injury and pain inflicted by them on each other.

	“Andy and Lukas build a traditional boyhood kind of friendship, and then Maya comes in. She brings in something very different. She brings in her own vulnerability. More and more they open up and these rituals develop. They build this safe space where they can show their wounds [both physical and psychological] and find some kind of healing for themselves, where they can feel seen and be who they are, being able to show their weaknesses.”

	The “Oasis” of the film’s title isn’t the forest, Lenz says. “It’s not a geographical place. It’s more something they create by themselves, by their togetherness, and by the trust and safe place they build together.”

	The director encouraged his young actors to feel their own way into the scenes in the forest, which they did with the help of an intimacy coordinator. The idea was to allow the actors to build trust with each other and the director.

	“I think these were very demanding scenes, so it was very important for me to bring them and their own ways of seeing it in,” Lenz says. “We started on a theoretical level, just reading the scenes and talking about it, building up trust with each other, and also trying to understand our personal reading of what we will develop here, and then, in the next step, when it got physical, I brought in an intimacy coordinator, who helped us a lot on how we can go on with that.

	“And it was very beautiful because when we had the first rehearsal, it was in a classical rehearsal room, so nothing very special. But when we left this theoretical stage and moved over to the physical stage, there was already such a big trust toward each other. So, they were not talking at all; they were just moving and touching with the hands, and asking questions with their eyes, like, ‘Is that okay? Can I move further? Should I stop? Something like this?’ And that was very touching for me to see that what we’ve worked out on a theoretical basis worked so well in a physical way. That was for me the moment when I really felt that we are onto something that’s worth sharing with other people.”
	

	Before he and his co-screenwriter and cinematographer, Alexander Dirninger, entered production, they set themselves various restrictions. For example, they chose to use as little dialogue as possible, forcing their actors to communicate non-verbally as far as possible, which adds an extra charge to every look, expression and touch.

	In the production notes, Lenz mentions that he grew up close to the site of the Winnenden school massacre in 2009. “The questions it raised — about fear and exclusion, about what happens to young people who can’t find their place — never fully left me,” he says. But anyone expecting to find a “birth of a killer” narrative will be disappointed. The film is far more subtle, nuanced and ambiguous than that.

	“Oasis” includes a scene in which an instructor in anti-violence techniques is brought in to help de-escalate the tensions, and another where a councillor encourages Andy to discuss the issues he’s facing. Both suggest that German society is trying to adopt new ways to lower the temperature. And Lukas’ father is at pains to cope with the situation without resorting to archaic methods of patriarchal control.

	The parents of the other students are keen to press for the exclusion of Andy. “What drives them is fear,” Lenz says. “Fear that something will happen to their children.” He adds, “The way they are behaving and the way they are dealing with the situation isn’t ideal, but it was very important for me to take each and every person in the film seriously — to understand their motivation, why they are behaving like that — and not to judge them and not to have something like the good guys and the bad guys.”

schema.headline: Teens Seek to Heal Wounds Through Macabre Rituals in Jannis Lenz’s ‘Oasis,’ With Hints of the Influence of Jessica Hausner, Michael Haneke

title: Mexico’s Venice Queer Lion Contender ‘Tijuana, Todavía’ Trains a Spotlight on the Plight of a Gay Refugee Fleeing Persecution
description: Nothing sharpens the mind like working within constraints. Made on a shoestring production grant of €200,000 ($234,000) and given three weeks to wri
body:
Nothing sharpens the mind like working within constraints. Made on a shoestring production grant of €200,000 ($234,000) and given three weeks to write a screenplay and outline a production schedule, ‘Tijuana, Todavía’ by Mexico’s Gabriel Gutiérrez Morales has been rewarded with a slot at the 83rd Venice Film Festival where it vies for the Queer Lion.

	All in all, Gutiérrez Morales and his producer-lead Humberto Busto (“Amores Perros”) were given 10 months to develop, write, produce, shoot and complete the film by the Biennale College – Cinema, which backed it as part of its annual training program. “Not even the smallest films in Mexico are made with a budget that tiny but at the same time, all those restrictions made it a very joyful experience,” said Busto.
	

	Not unlike David Pablo’s Queer Lion and Horizons winner last year, which represents Mexico at the 2027 Oscars, “Tijuana, Todavía” (translated to “Still, Tijuana”) takes place in northern Mexico, specifically the titular border town of Tijuana.  


	 “Tijuana, Todavía” follows the fraught relationship between Maksim, a young queer man who has fled Russia to avoid being drafted into the war with Ukraine, and Chava, a middle-aged gay man grappling with the culture of Northern Mexican machismo.

	“As a producer and performer, I feel this film arrives at a pivotal moment,” said Busto, who plays Chava. ‘Tijuana, Todavía’ speaks directly to the current situation in Russia and to the consequences of queer migration to countries like Mexico. This experience of displacement and reinvention at the border is the core identity of the film.” 
	

	Busto adds: “As queer filmmakers, we are particularly concerned by the constant threats to our community and that is why we want to counter with this film and establish a dialogue.”

	He pointed to recent news that the Italian Ministry of Culture, now under a right-wing government, was not going to support the Queer Lion for the first time in its 20-year history.

	Said Gutiérrez: “To add to what Humberto was saying, we felt the need to tell this story and we had the real-life background for it. But then the question became: why set a film like this at the border in Tijuana? Why make the protagonist a Russian refugee?

	“The border has been part of conversations around immigration for years. But especially since Trump’s presidency, it’s often portrayed almost like a war zone. What you rarely get to see is the border from the other side. That always felt absurd to me because Tijuana is where I grew up.”

	Tapping his own life experience was key. “One of the seeds for the film came when I was still living in Tijuana, shortly after I came out. I struggled to find community in person, so I had a lot of online friends. There was a certain sense of safety in being behind a screen. One of those friends was a gay man from St. Petersburg, Russia and we’ve been friends for about 10 years now.”

	Given their budget constraints, the challenge in finding a Russian actor in Mexico to play Maksim was slim but as serendipity would have it, they found Petr Filimonov whose life experience closely mirrored that of Maksim. Like his fictional character, Filimonov was a refugee. He had been arrested for his opposition to the Ukraine war and being gay made him even a bigger target so he fled soon after his family secured his release. He now resides in Mexico.

	“In our second interview with him, Petr was visibly emotional, with tears in his eyes. He said: ‘I’m Maksim. I’ve traveled all this way because this is a story you wrote, without even knowing me.’ And to add to their luck, he had also been studying acting for the past four years in Russia. “It was incredibly powerful to watch him and know that, even though this was fiction, his heart and his own experiences were right there in the film,” said Busto.

	Reality also reflected art in the case of the Casa de Luz refugee shelter that they featured in the film. “Incredibly, the founder had a personal experience that almost mirrored the story. She fell in love with a Russian man who came to the shelter in a situation similar to the one in the film. Trump’s administration deported him to Egypt and she spent months following him through Egypt, Turkey, the Philippines and Thailand. They eventually got married and finally reunited just a few days before we started shooting. It was an extraordinary real-life parallel to the story we were telling,” Busto related.
	

	Produced by Fosfo Producciones and distributed in Mexico by Colmena, the film also stars Miry Rodríguez, Dilan Rivera, Elliot Roy Rensky and Jorge Domínguez Cerdá.

schema.headline: Mexico’s Venice Queer Lion Contender ‘Tijuana, Todavía’ Trains a Spotlight on the Plight of a Gay Refugee Fleeing Persecution

title: ‘Chronovisor’ Review: An Eerie, Fiendishly Clever Mystery for Lovers of Libraries and the Storied Smell of Old Books
description: For anyone whose happy place is an old-school library reading room, all aged dark wood and green-and-gold reading lamps casting warm islands of ligh
body:
For anyone whose happy place is an old-school library reading room, all aged dark wood and green-and-gold reading lamps casting warm islands of light in the velvety murk, “Chronovisor” will be a near-fetishistic delight — even as it makes quite unhappy places of such hallowed havens of learning. The first feature by U.S. writer-directors Jack Auen and Kevin Walker builds on the studied lo-fi style of their well-regarded 2021 short “Marblehead,” doing an awful lot with very little as they fashion an ornate, occult-inflected sci-fi film from the pages of various yellowed academic volumes: not adapting them, let it be said, but reading them, and making us do the same, in ways that prove eerily atmospheric and surprisingly riveting.
	

	A conversation-stoking standout at this year’s Rotterdam festival in January, now getting a limited U.S. theatrical release through Grasshopper Films, “Chronovisor” is an undeniably niche proposition, though it’s also easy to make the film sound more dustily recherché than it is. The prospect of a research-based mystery told heavily through text, which the film undeniably is, probably won’t get many people’s pulses racing. But add that it’s also a semi-factual inquiry bridging time-travel theory and Vatican conspiracies, with a side shot of Ivy League “Blair Witch” horror styling, and perhaps more viewers will be open to its weird, obsessive trickery. Either way, it’s the kind of wildly sui generis film made to foster its own fascinated, slow-growing cult — and puts Auen and Walker on the map as mischievous genre mixologists to watch.
	

	Their devotion to knotty specifics of academia extends to casting a real-life academic — Anne-Laure Sellier,  currently a professor of behavioral sciences at HEC Paris business school — in the lead. It’s a stunt that pays off in two ways: First, unlike in the vast majority of genre films set in the university realm, the film’s intellectual exchanges don’t sound hopelessly phony; and second, she has the nervous, recessive, slightly out-of-place quality necessary to set the story in motion. She plays Beatrice, a French scholar of philosophy and neuroscience at Columbia, introduced in conversation with another academic in a low-lit New York restaurant — an exchange of ideas that never blooms into personal chemistry, which seems to be the general way of things in her world.

	She’s more at home, unsurprisingly, with her research papers and stacks of books, as she pursues an elusive breakthrough on the neurology of memory — in the process becoming fixated on the real-life history of the Chronovisor, an alleged 1970s invention of Italian Benedictine monk Pellegrino Ernetti, that he outlandishly boasted could retrieve first-hand silent video from any point in the past, extending even to footage of Christ’s crucifixion. Though it was largely debunked as a hoax, Beatrice can’t quite let go of this curious lore, chasing and wheedling information out of various Ernetti-adjacent sources, until finally connecting with a European scientist who claims to have had a very real, mind-melting experience with the machine.

	It’s all highly elaborate hokum that “Chronovisor” treats with deliciously tongue-in-cheek studiousness — Dan Brown dressed in the most elevated language of Umberto Eco. But while there’s a lurid thrill to the film’s ultimate revelations, drolly taken down a peg by the anticlimactically dingy aesthetic of VHS-era imagery, the film’s principal pleasures lie in the actual gathering of information: As Beatrice pores over forgotten leather-bound volumes, the salient words are illuminated and translated for the viewer’s edification, elegantly overlaid upon the filmed page — following the creases and curves of the paper — to precisely replicate the protagonist’s reading experience, so we share in her eureka moments along the way. 

	Rarely has a film so resourcefully evoked the transportive but decidedly analog thrill of reading; rarely has the warmly musty smell of research libraries and archives somehow wafted with such sense-memory precision off a cinema screen. “Chronovisor” is richly alive to the audiovisual tools of its own medium: Leo Zhang’s wonderfully tactile 16mm cinematography revels in the bleary glow of isolated lightbulbs late at night, winking through spilled-ink lakes of shadow, while the soundtrack wittily samples the grand orchestral mysticism of the late English composer Gustav Holst and the pompous kitsch of Gregorian chants. With this alternately silly, frightening, forward-looking and rampantly nostalgic puzzle piece, Auen and Walker show themselves to be in thrall to the printed word, and all the winding imaginative alleys it can lead you down — but they remain filmmakers first and foremost, and rather good ones at that.

schema.headline: ‘Chronovisor’ Review: An Eerie, Fiendishly Clever Mystery for Lovers of Libraries and the Storied Smell of Old Books

title: Al Pacino Sends Video Message to Venice After Missing Press Conference for ‘Father Joe’: ‘I Wish I Was There, I Really Do’
description: Al Pacino didn’t travel to the Venice Film Festival for the premiere of “Father Joe,” but he sent a video message with well wishes to his collaborat
body:
Al Pacino didn’t travel to the Venice Film Festival for the premiere of “Father Joe,” but he sent a video message with well wishes to his collaborators on the movie.

	“I wish I was there with all of you in Venice, which is great and lovely. I’ve had films there. I’ve been there. I’ve experienced it,” said a sunglass-clad Pacino before he shouted out writer-producer Luc Besson (“It’s great to say his name”) and his co-star Kiefer Sutherland. “Have a good one. Best to you all.”
	


	“Father Joe,” starring Sutherland, Pacino and Ever Anderson, takes place in 1990s Manhattan’s Little Italy and revolves around a priest who clashes with a mob boss. The action-thriller was written and produced by Besson and marks the directing debut of Barthélémy Grossmann. Grossmann has referred to “Father Joe” as a “modern fable about faith, redemption and the complexity of human nature.”


	Sutherland plays the titular Father Joe, described as “a man of God unlike any other” who wages a secret war — singlehandedly busting crime rings and turning the city’s underworld into his congregation. Pacino plays a powerful crime lord whose empire collides with Father Joe’s crusade. Anderson portrays a young woman caught between danger and redemption under Joe’s guidance. 

	Sutherland said he was drawn to the project — which he called a meditation on “good vs. evil” — because of Besson’s involvement.

	“I was a huge, huge fan,” Sutherland said. “Luc had made films I wish I had been in. I thought, ‘That is the kind of movie I should be making.’ But he never hired me. Very fortunately, he thought of me for this idea.”
	

	Besson is the influential French director of “The Fifth Element,” “Lucy” and most recently, a “Dracula” remake starring Caleb Landry Jones and Christoph Waltz. He one of the first prominent figures in France to face sexual assault allegations in the #MeToo era. He was accused of rape by Belgian-Dutch female actor Sand Van Roy, though Besson was eventually cleared of all charges.

	Besson described a hands-off style as a producer on “Father Joe.”

	“The good thing is I’m also a director. I don’t want to be bothered when I’m a director so I tried not to bother,” Besson said. “I’m on the back of Barthélémy. As long as he doesn’t have a problem, I’m not there.”

schema.headline: Al Pacino Sends Video Message to Venice After Missing Press Conference for ‘Father Joe’: ‘I Wish I Was There, I Really Do’

title: ‘Primetime’ Review: Robert Pattinson Leads a Dazzling Cast in a Lurid Horror-Movie Portrait of a ‘Predator’-Hunter’s Predatory Instinct
description: “Can you get tighter in on him?” Chris Hansen (Robert Pattinson) demands of the technician editing his latest “To Catch a Predator” segment. He has
body:
“Can you get tighter in on him?” Chris Hansen (Robert Pattinson) demands of the technician editing his latest “To Catch a Predator” segment. He has noticed that when his would-be pedophile prey finally spot him, stepping out of an upstairs bedroom or strolling through the kitchen door of the house designed to ensnare evildoers like them, their nostrils tend to flare. Hansen wants that quiver to read onscreen. He thinks people will like to see it. Perhaps in the very same spirit of ghoulish voyeurism, director Lance Oppenheim has designed “Primetime” as a nightmarishly claustrophobic 4:3 portrait of Hansen as a horror villain, macro-zoomed-in as if, past the point of image degradation, approaching the point at which the portrait becomes all but unrecognisable as a human being, we might be able to peer through the sickly sheen of his skin, dive in through one of his pores and see his very soul. Or the place where his soul once, presumably, lived. 
	

	In DP David Bolen’s greasy, saturated images, so livid with grain that it feels like they leave dirt under your fingernails, the film begins in 2006 when then-NBC head Jeff Zucker (played, in quite the coup, by Jeff Zucker) calls Hansen and his producer Andie (Merritt Wever) into a meeting. In response to public demand, and rather against Zucker’s own stated preferences, their show, previously a part of NBC’s “Dateline,” is being moved to its own primetime slot, where it will slug it out for ratings against ABC’s juggernaut “Lost.” 


	In an interesting incidental parallel with the newspaper rivalry outlined in Danny Boyle’s Venice opener “Ink” — another portrait of a media man driven beyond the bounds of morality, with similarly fatal consequences — the desire to surpass “Lost’s” viewership numbers becomes an obsession for Hansen, even though he has distractions aplenty. His relationship with his wife (Anna Faris) and kids is disintegrating and a National Enquirer journo keeps threatening to run an exposé of his infidelities. Meanwhile Andie is being headhunted by a rival show on another network, and newly recruited “decoy” Dan (Skyler Gisondo) is trying hard to square his naive dreams of acting stardom with his role as the show’s resident underage bait. Then Hansen hears that, in Texas, a potential “whale” (ie. a person of political importance) has maybe taken that bait, and he makes a series of increasingly rash decisions to pursue the man at all costs.
	

	Daniel Garber’s inspired, allusive and often very witty editing style constantly makes illuminating connections and interruptions. But otherwise, this uncompromisingly grimy approach would be actively repellent were it not for the extraordinary performances, which make “Primetime” a thing you cannot stop watching even as the desire to flee to the nearest shower cubicle grows. 

	Most obviously, front and center, and in endlessly intrusive close-up, there’s Pattinson — who also serves as producer — playing the arrogant, fame-addicted, megalomaniac Hansen. Pattinson’s mimicry of the real Hansen’s physical mannerisms, like the awkward staging of his gotcha moments while he clutches a sheaf of damning chatroom printouts, is one thing. But his vocal impersonation, capturing the self-consciously over-rehearsed cadences of Hansen’s speech, is uncanny. The film’s excellent soundscape, powered by Ari Balouzian’s throbbing, queasy score, often features snatches of Hansen trying out different deliveries of deeply ick messages from the groomer-of-the-moment. “I will undress you; you will undress me,” he murmurs repeatedly over black as the opening titles end.

	But Pattinson’s is only one turn within a stellar cast who individually deliver some career-best screen work. In particular Wever, who has never not been good in anything, is absolutely blistering here, as Hansen’s undervalued, gum-snapping, shark-eyed producer — perhaps less of a sociopath than Hansen only because she has less influence. And who is worse, anyway: the madman who practically cannot stop himself marching further towards the gates of hell, or the perfectly sane pragmatist who elects, in full possession of her faculties, to ride on his coattails all the way there? 

	Beyond Wever, there are revelatory turns from a very moving Gisondo, and from singer Phoebe Bridgers, whose character, Del, regards her decoy position as “a form of activism” against child abusers. Bridgers proffers the second of the film’s most impressive transformations when Del is occasionally pressed into service to perform as an underage boy — changing her body language, her gait and, again, her voice. But there are really no weak links in the chain of performances here, from Tony Revolori, Jonathan Lipnicki and Alex Winter (superb) in the unenviable roles of the quote-unquote predators, to Matthew Maher as the wildly overzealous researcher with the Perverted Justice group, without whose expertise in luring pedophiles out from behind their computer screens, the “To Catch a Predator” phenomenon never could have happened.
	

	So how did it all happen? That’s a question that “Primetime” doesn’t really care to answer — and one better addressed in David Osit’s excellent 2025 documentary “Predators.” With its narrow focus on Hansen’s progressive psychological disintegration, there is little room outside “Primetime’s”‘ cramped, feverish frames for anything like context, and its only real attempt is perhaps the film’s only misstep. We’re asked to believe that Hansen developed a child-snatching-monster mythology during a trip to India in the ’90s, which gives the film its most overt genre-horror imagery but also implies he has an actual system of belief — a code of honor, however skewed — when elsewhere, he is more convincingly characterized as a void, wrapped in an ego so overweeningly ambitious that his only belief is in himself.

	It’s amusing to consider that Pattinson is also the star of “The Batman,” when the Hansen of “Primetime” can be read as a self-styled Dark Knight of vigilante justice, suffering from a kind of White Knight syndrome, by which he mistakes the adulation of the TV-watching public for actual moral rectitude. (Yet he is still petty enough to phone the helpline number on the vending machine that has failed to dispense his snack. Who does that? Of all the many seedy little features of Hansen’s interior landscape, that may just be the most disturbing, as well as the funniest.) “There used to be a pillory in every civilized town,” Hansen tells Dan, while the lighting illuminates his white teeth and makes empty black holes of his eyes, “but now there’s a TV in every home.” “Primetime” does a unsettlingly effective job of explaining how that kind of ubiquity can drive a man to the brink of insanity. But it never swings its ravenous camera back on us; perhaps Oppenheim knows we’re not ready for what it would reveal.

title: How Maggie Gyllenhaal Used Dakota Johnson and Ellen Burstyn to Reimagine Marilyn Monroe at 100 in Venice Short ‘Flesh Impact’
description: Marilyn Monroe would have turned 100 this year. So when Maggie Gyllenhaal was approached to make a movie about her, she asked for a weekend to daydr
body:
Marilyn Monroe would have turned 100 this year. So when Maggie Gyllenhaal was approached to make a movie about her, she asked for a weekend to daydream about what that milestone might look like. What came back was “Flesh Impact,” a 17-minute short that hands the most consumed movie star of the 20th century something she was rarely granted in life — the floor to speak her mind.

	The film premieres at the Venice Film Festival, where Gyllenhaal is also serving as president of this year’s competition jury. Variety is exclusively debuting a clip from the short below.
	

	Gyllenhaal didn’t arrive at Monroe on her own. Genesis, which commissioned the short to mark the centennial, came to her with a deceptively simple brief. “They came to me and said, ‘Could you make a movie about Marilyn Monroe where Marilyn Monroe is given the opportunity to express something, to articulate herself as an artist in a way that she was not given when she was alive?’” Gyllenhaal recalls. “I said, ‘Let me daydream about it for a weekend and if I can, I will and if I can’t, I won’t waste your time.’ And what came to me was this idea of her at 100. I thought, there’s no way they’re going to want that. But they did.”

	The conceit — Monroe imagined at the century mark, walking into an audition and finally allowed to speak her mind — arrived nearly whole. So did its length. Conceived from the start as a film of five to 20 minutes, the project suited a director who has never been drawn to sprawl. “I actually have quite a few little stories in my mind that should be shorts,” she says. “The ones in my head are not five minutes; they’re usually like 20 minutes. This was always the right length for this.”
	

	She builds the story around an audition, an engine she chose for its raw exposure. “Auditioning is very vulnerable, because in order to do it well, you have to risk everything — your whole heart and body — and yet you know you could be told no at any moment.”

	“Flesh Impact” is, in part, a film about Gyllenhaal’s first vocation. A two-time Oscar nominee who has spent the past several years behind the camera, she treats performance itself as the subject. “Acting, and maybe particularly being an actress, when seen very deeply and from a compassionate place, is an unusual job,” she says.

	The title comes from Billy Wilder, who once described a quality Monroe had on-screen — the sense that you could reach out and touch her. Gyllenhaal both honors the observation and interrogates it. In the passage that gives the film its name, Dakota Johnson moves through the frame as the younger Monroe in a sheer nightgown and Gyllenhaal wants the audience to feel the pull before it feels the ache. “I’m hoping that it’s appealing, compelling, sexy,” she says. “And then, once you know what Billy Wilder was talking about, feel it from the perspective of the person whose body we’re talking about. It’s just a more complicated thing than you might think at first.”

	Casting Johnson was, by Gyllenhaal’s own admission, a provocation. Johnson doesn’t look like Monroe — and that turned out to be the point. “At first I was slightly unsure about it,” she says. “And then I thought, I don’t actually know what Marilyn Monroe looks like, because she’s been so dehumanized. There’s the snow globe. There’s the poster on Hollywood Boulevard. Her real face almost feels a little blurry to me, and I think that’s probably true for a lot of people. I’m much more interested in where the cracks are and humanity can seep through.”

	Sharing the role, as the centenarian Monroe of the audition, is Academy Award winner Ellen Burstyn, who will collect the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at this year’s festival — a coronation Gyllenhaal gets to savor from the jury table.

	Peter Sarsgaard, Gyllenhaal’s husband and constant collaborator, anchors the audition room. The ensemble extends to a former “Deuce” castmate, Sepideh Moafi — a current Emmy nominee for “The Pitt” — in a nearly wordless role Gyllenhaal insists lingers. “She doesn’t speak a lot, but we’re going to be in your mind as much as anyone else’s,” she says.
	

	For a director who works fast, the shorthand mattered more than the schedule. Gyllenhaal reassembled much of the crew from her feature “The Bride!” — reuniting with cinematographer Lawrence Sher and cutting the film with her “Lost Daughter” editor, Affonso Gonçalves. “It was so nice to already have a shorthand,” she says. “If I’m going to make a movie super quickly, I want to work with people I already have a language with.”

	Speed had its costs. The production planned to grab exterior footage outside Broadway’s Music Box Theatre — the film’s principal location — before a New York City blizzard intervened. “So we got absolutely fucked,” she says, chuckling. The team decamped for a single day on the Paramount lot in Los Angeles. “It was January,” she says, “so there was no way we could ask Dakota to walk in a negligee just anywhere.”

	Though the story is set now, Gyllenhaal reached for the texture of another era. “I felt it had almost an early-’80s quality, or late-’70s — like when Broadway theater was really alive,” she says, citing the backstage worlds of “All That Jazz” and “A Chorus Line.” (She also nods to “Tootsie.”) “There’s so much great stuff on stage now, but there’s a much more corporate aspect to things. I wanted that feeling.”

	Gyllenhaal holds a special place in her heart for Venice. She premiered “The Lost Daughter” there during the pandemic, having never screened it in any room before. “That is where I felt I was born as a director,” she says.

	This year she returns wearing two hats and keeping them deliberately apart. As for acting, it remains on the shelf. “It’s just not where my head is,” she says. “I’m much more interested at the moment in writing and directing. It feels like an opportunity for a much more complete kind of expression.”

	Two projects have stayed with her — one an adaptation, one not — and she plans to start writing once the festival is behind her. “I’m giving myself the next few weeks of Venice off,” she says.

	For a filmmaker who built 17 minutes around the ache of being watched, there’s a quiet symmetry to it — a stretch on the Lido spent, for once, doing the looking herself.

title: Aaron Rodgers Hopes to Start Family After Retirement From NFL
body:
Aaron Rodgers
                          Ready for Fatherhood!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 4, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Aaron Rodgers is looking forward to retirement ... and says he hopes to start a family with his wife.
      
    
            The Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback opened up about his future during an interview with SiriusXM's "Mad Dog Sports Radio," saying he's hoping to be "supporting my pregnant wife" by this time next year.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Rodgers said he and his wife, publicly known as Brittani, plan to start a family after he steps away from football following the 2026 season.
      
    
            "I'm looking forward to a life of quiet after 22 years in the pros and three in college," he said ... adding he's also focused on healing his body and building a family.
      

            Rodgers later clarified he and Brittani are not currently expecting but said fatherhood is the next chapter he’s most excited about.
      
    
            He says he enjoys being "Uncle Aaron" to his brother's children and said spending time with them has made both him and his wife more eager to have kids of their own.
      
    
            Rodgers confirmed in May the 2026 NFL season will be his last. He previously revealed he secretly married Brittani in 2025 ... but has kept details about their relationship largely private.
